newsitem.title: GERMANY: Angry German miners protest at government cut plans.
newsitem.headline: Angry German miners protest at government cut plans.

text.p: German coal miners staged angry protests on Friday after Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government proposed slashing federal subsidies to their beleaguered industry.

Thousands of miners in the Ruhr river mining region walked off the job on Friday after union leaders said the government was determined to cut annual subsidies from 10 billion marks ($5.8 billion) to 3.8 billion marks over the next eight years.
A group of 50 helmeted miners formed a barricade across a motorway near Duisburg and only agreed to end their protest after IG Bergbau mining union leaders ordered them off the autobahn.
"We are worried that there will be an escalation of these types of demonstrations," a union spokesman said.
Miners also threateneed to occupy coal mines in Gelsenkirchen, Herne, Recklinghausen and Dorsten. More and more miners were walking out during the day, the spokesman said.

Under pressure to rein in budget deficits, Kohl's centre-right coalition government on Thursday said it could provide the coal mining industry with annual subisidies totalling 3.8 billion marks from 2005.
"This is a generous offer," Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl said.
Kohl made the offer at a meeting between ministers and the head of the IG Bergbau miners union aimed at reaching a compromise on the level of aid following the expiry of the current agreement.

The government, straining to qualify for Europe's single currency, now pays 10 billion marks in aid each year to support more than 90,000 jobs. Union leaders fear the subsidy cuts mean 45,000 jobs would be lost, further exacerbating unemployment in an already depressed region.
"The government has a responsibility to taxpayers," said Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt. "Every mining job is now being subsidised by taxpayers to the tune of 135,000 marks."

The miners union said ahead of the meeting it could accept a cut in aid to around 6.5 billion marks but that this would mean keeping just 12 coalfields in operation and reducing the number of jobs in the industry to around 50,000.
Wolfgang Clement, economics minister of North Rhine-Westphalia state, rejected Bonn's offer and accused the conservative chancellor of partisian politics.
"What the federal government is trying to pull off is absolutely unacceptable and won't be tolerated," Clement said.
"I seriously doubt the government would try to pull a stunt like this in Bavaria or Baden-Wuerttemberg. The government is trying to dump its financial problems on us."

Germany's main mining regions are in the states of North Rhine-Westphalia and the Saar, both of which are ruled by the Social Democrats (SPD), the main opposition in Bonn. Bavaria and Baden-Wuerttemberg are controlled by the conservative Christian Democrats and Christian Social Union.
About 200,000 miners and their supporters last month formed a 100 km (60 mile) human chain through the Ruhr Valley to protest against the planned cuts in aid.

German hard coal, which comes from deep mines, is more expensive than imports. But Bonn has sought to use subsidies to protect jobs in the region and keep the mines operating. ($ = 1.713 German Marks)
